posts.central_knowledge_unit: Ulama, a 3,400-year-old ballgame that survived in Mexico | AP News
posts.claim: Ulama—especially ulama de cadera in Sinaloa—is a living, endangered descendant/tradition of the pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican ballgame. The wider ballgame tradition has archaeological evidence reaching at least the second millennium BCE (including a formal court dated about 1650 BCE), so describing the tradition as roughly 3,400–3,500 years old is reasonable; that dating should not be presented as proof that today’s ulama has remained unchanged for that entire period.
posts.headline: Ulama de Cadera: Ancient Mexican Ballgame Endures in Sinaloa

posts.central_knowledge_unit: Origins of the Mesoamerican ballgame: Earliest ballcourt from the highlands found at Etlatongo, Oaxaca, Mexico | Science Advances
posts.claim: The ballgame represents one of the most enduring and iconic features of ancient Mesoamerican civilization, yet its origins and evolution remain poorly understood, primarily associated with the Gulf Coast and southern Pacific coastal lowlands. While one early ballcourt dates to 1650 BCE from the Chiapas lowlands, ballcourts have remained undocumented in the Mesoamerican highlands until a millennium later, suggesting less involvement by highland civilizations in the ballgame’s evolution. We provide new data from the southern highlands of Mexico, from the Early Formative period (1500–1000 BCE), that necessitate revising previous paradigms.
